title: Pearson vs Spearman Scoring Panel
takeaway: The paper re-runs its automated interpretability scoring with Pearson correlation alongside the Spearman correlation used throughout the main text, and the two give visibly the same distributions and the same ordering: dictionary-learning features score well above transformer neurons, while features from a randomized model sit awkwardly high. This is a check that the headline gap does not depend on which correlation coefficient was chosen, not a new measurement.
walkthrough:
You are looking at a 4x3 grid of histograms. Each of the four stacked blocks is one *way of scoring* a unit. Each of the three columns is one *population* of units being scored.

### Reading the grid

The columns are fixed all the way down. Left: features from dictionary learning run A/1 ([[feature-notation]] — model A, autoencoder run 1). Middle: the MLP neurons of that same transformer, the [[polysemanticity]] baseline. Right: features learned by running the same autoencoder on a [[randomized-transformer]], whose weights were shuffled so that any structure comes from the data rather than from training.

Row 1 is the [[manual-interpretability-scoring]] result: a count of scored activation intervals at each value of the 0–14 [[feature-interpretability-rubric]]. Rows 2–4 plot density, so bar heights integrate to one and panels are comparable even though the populations differ in size.

Rows 2 and 3 are the same [[automated-interpretability]] experiment scored twice. Claude writes an explanation of a unit from examples, then uses only that explanation to predict the unit's activations on unseen tokens; the score is the correlation between predicted and true activations. Row 2 uses [[pearson-correlation]]. Row 3 uses [[spearman-correlation]], the rank-based version reported everywhere in the main text. Row 4 is [[automated-logit-scoring]], an accuracy rather than a correlation.

The triangle under each panel marks that distribution's median. The dotted vertical line marks the null value: zero correlation in rows 2–3, chance accuracy of $0.5$ in row 4.

### What it shows

Compare row 2 against row 3, panel by panel. The shapes track each other closely: the same spike at zero, the same long climb toward $1.0$ for features, the same narrow pile-up at zero for neurons. Medians move by a few hundredths and never change the ranking.

That is the whole point of the figure. Pearson is included only so the numbers can be set beside Bills et al., whose autointerp scores are Pearson correlations; the paper's own conclusions were computed on Spearman.

The comparison the reader should carry away is between columns, not rows. Features beat neurons under either coefficient. The randomized column beating features on correlation is discussed separately, and the paper attributes it to easy single-token features rather than to real interpretability.

terms.definition: The left column: features learned by the sparse autoencoder run labelled A/1, meaning transformer A and dictionary learning run 1. This is the run whose features the paper studies throughout the main text.

The middle column: the ordinary MLP neurons of transformer A, scored by exactly the same procedures as the features. They are the baseline the paper wants to beat, because individual neurons are expected to be polysemantic.

The right column: features from running the same dictionary learning on a version of transformer A whose weight matrices have had their entries shuffled. It tests how much of the structure found comes from the dataset alone rather than from a trained model.

The top row's title: scores assigned by a blinded human annotator who formed an interpretation of each unit and rated it on a fixed rubric. The paper treats human judgment as the metric it trusts most.

The x-axis of the top row: the total score on the paper's interpretability rubric, summing confidence in the interpretation, consistency of high activations with it, consistency of the logit weights with it, an effect-size separation point, and specificity.
The y-axis of the top row: the raw number of scored activation intervals falling in each rubric bin. It is a count rather than a density because the human sample is small.

The scoring pipeline behind rows 2, 3 and 4: a language model (Claude) writes an explanation of a unit from examples, and that explanation alone is then used to predict behaviour the model has not seen.

Row 2's metric: the ordinary linear correlation between Claude's predicted activations and the true activations, across the scored tokens for one unit. Included only for comparability with Bills et al., who scored this way.

Row 3's metric: the same comparison computed on ranks instead of raw values, so it measures whether Claude gets the ordering of activations right rather than their magnitudes. This is the metric used throughout the paper's main text.
The x-axis of rows 2 and 3: one unit's score, ranging from -0.4 to 1.0 as plotted. Each bar counts units, not tokens; every feature or neuron contributes exactly one correlation value.
The y-axis of rows 2, 3 and 4: a normalised histogram height, so the area under each panel is one. It lets panels with different numbers of units be compared directly.

The bottom row's metric: from the same explanation, Claude labels each candidate output token yes or no for whether the unit firing should make that token more likely. It cross-checks the explanation against what the unit does, not just when it fires.
The x-axis of the bottom row: the fraction of logit tokens Claude classified correctly for one unit, on a set that is half true top-positive logits and half random tokens.

The legend entry for the small triangles beneath each panel, each marking the median score of that panel's distribution. Medians are used rather than means because several distributions are strongly skewed or bimodal.
The reference line drawn in rows 2 through 4. In the correlation rows it sits at zero correlation; in the logit row it sits at 0.5, which is chance for a balanced yes/no task.

One of eleven evenly spaced bands between zero and a unit's maximum activation, sampled from so that scoring covers the whole activation spectrum rather than only the top examples. The top row counts intervals, not units.

The tall thin bar exactly at 0 in rows 2 and 3. When Claude predicts a constant value, most often all zeros, no correlation is defined and the paper assigns a score of zero, which piles units up at that point.
The language model used as the automated interpreter: it produces the explanations and then makes the activation and logit predictions that rows 2 through 4 score.
The prior automated-interpretability work whose scoring protocol this paper adapts. Its scores are Pearson correlations, which is why row 2 exists at all.

numbers.meaning: The grid layout: four scoring methods (manual rubric, Pearson autointerp, Spearman autointerp, logit-weight accuracy) crossed with three populations (A/1 features, A neurons, randomized-model features).
The range of the manual rubric x-axis. The maximum is 14 rather than 15 because a perfect score on the effect-size-separation item makes the following item inapplicable.
The median rubric score for A/1 features (row 1, left triangle). The paper reads this as the annotator having a confident, specific, consistent hypothesis that also matched the logit weights.
The median rubric score for neurons (row 1, middle triangle), and the location of their tall spike. A zero means the annotator could not even form a hypothesis about what the neuron represents.

The approximate median rubric score for randomized-model features (row 1, right triangle). It sits between features and neurons because the randomized set is bimodal: a cluster at 0 plus a non-zero cluster.

The tallest bars in the top row: roughly 23 counts at rubric 13-14 for features, 23 at rubric 0 for neurons, and 23 at 0 for randomized features. Counts are small because human scoring is labour-intensive.
The total human workload behind row 1: 412 activation intervals scored across 162 features and neurons combined. This is why row 1 is plotted as counts, not density.
The plotted x-range of the two correlation rows. Correlations can in principle reach -1, but almost nothing falls below -0.4 in practice.
The median autointerp score for A/1 features under the two coefficients. They differ by a few hundredths, which is the figure's whole claim.
The median autointerp score for neurons under the two coefficients. Both sit far below the feature medians, so the feature-versus-neuron gap survives the change of metric.

The median autointerp score for randomized-model features, above the A/1 features under both coefficients. The paper attributes this to easy single-token features in the randomized model, not to genuine interpretability.

The height of the zero-correlation spike in the neuron panels of rows 2 and 3. It is the largest density in either correlation row, and reflects how often Claude's explanation of a neuron yields a constant prediction.

In the randomized-feature panels, the height of the spike at zero and the height of the peak near correlation 0.9 (about 3.2 under Pearson, about 2.85 under Spearman). That right-hand peak is the single-token cluster that is trivially easy to predict.
The evidence behind each single correlation value in rows 2 and 3: per unit, Claude predicts activations for 60 held-out dataset examples of nine tokens each.

The number of examples Claude is shown when writing an explanation: ten top-activation, two from each of the other 12 intervals, five random, and ten showing the top tokens in other contexts. These are kept separate from the 60 scoring examples.
The integer range activations are quantized to before Claude sees or predicts them, following Bills et al. It is why row 3's rank-based correlation is a natural fit for this data.
Chance accuracy in row 4, marked by the dotted line, because the logit set is a 50/50 mix of true top-positive logits and random tokens.

The medians in row 4 for A/1 features, neurons and randomized features. The randomized median sits exactly at chance, which follows from its weights being shuffled so its logit effects carry no structure.

The main text's version of the same logit result, quoted as averages across features and across neurons rather than medians. The average for neurons is higher than their median of 0.53 because the neuron distribution has a tail above chance.
The logit set scored per unit in row 4: 50 random vocabulary tokens plus the 10th through 60th largest positive logits. The top 10 are excluded because they were used to generate the explanation.

The height of the spike at accuracy 0.5 for randomized features in row 4, far taller than anything else in that row. Random weights give Claude nothing to be right or wrong about, so nearly every unit lands at chance.
